cards.definition: A set is a well-defined collection of objects; that is, it is defined in such a manner such that we can determine for any given object $x$ whether or not $x$ belongs to the set.
An element is any member of a set.
Two sets are equal if they contain exactly the same elements.
The cardinality of a set is the number of elements it has.
The empty set is the set $\{\}$ that contains no elements.
An ordered pair is a list $(x,y)$ of two things $x$ and $y$, enclosed in parentheses and separated by a comma. The order is significant; that is $(x,y) = (a,b)$ if and only if $x = a$ and $y = b$.
The Cartesian product of two sets $A$ and $B$ is another set, denoted as $A \times B$ and defined as $A \times B = \{(a,b) : a \in A, b \in B\}$.

For any set $A$ and a positive integer $n$, the Cartesian power$A^n$} is \[A^n =\underbrace{A \times A \times \cdots \times A}_\text{$n$ times} = \{(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n) : x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n \in A\}.\]

Suppose $A$ and $B$ are sets. If every element of $A$ is also an element of $B$, then we say $A$ is a subset of $B$, and we denote this as $A \subseteq B$. We write $A \not\subseteq B$ if $A$ is not a subset of $B$.
If $A$ is a set, the power set of $A$ is another set, denoted as $\mathcal{P}(A)$ and defined to be the set of all subsets of $A$. In symbols, \[\mathcal{P}(A) = \{X : X \subseteq A\}.\]
Suppose $A$ and $B$ are sets. The union of $A$ and $B$ is the set \[A\cup B = \{x : x \in A \text{ or } x \in B\}.\]
Suppose $A$ and $B$ are sets. The intersection of $A$ and $B$ is the set \[A\cap B = \{x : x \in A \text{ and } x \in B\}.\]
Suppose $A$ and $B$ are sets. The difference of $A$ and $B$ is the set \[A - B = \{x : x \in A \text{ and } x \not\in B\}.\]
The universal set is a set fixed within the framework of a theory and consisting of all objects considered in this theory.
Let $A$ be a set with a universal set $U$. The complement of $A$ denoted $\overline{A}$, is the set \[\overline{A} = U - A.\]
An index set is a set whose members index the elements of another set.

Suppose $A_1,A_2,\ldots,A_n$ are sets. Then
\[\emph{A_1\cup A_2 \cup \cdots \cup A_n} = \{x : x \in A_i \text{ for at least one set } A_i, \text{ for } 1 \leq i \leq n\}.\]

Suppose $A_1,A_2,\ldots,A_n$ are sets. Then
\[\emph{A_1\cap A_2 \cap \cdots \cap A_n} = \{x : x \in A_i \text{ for every set } A_i, \text{ for } 1 \leq i \leq n\}.\]

Suppose $\{A_i\}_{i \in \N}$ is a family of sets. Then
\[\emph{\bigcup_{i=1}^\infty A_i} = A_1\cup A_2 \cup \cdots = \{x : x \in A_i \text{ for at least one set } A_i, \text{ with } 1 \leq i\}.\]

Suppose $\{A_i\}_{i \in \N}$ is a family of sets. Then
\[\emph{\bigcap_{i=1}^\infty A_i} = A_1\cap A_2 \cap \cdots = \{x : x \in A_i \text{ for every } A_i, \text{ with } 1 \leq i\}.\]

If $A_\alpha$ is a set for every $\alpha$ in some index set $I \neq \varnothing$, then
\[\emph{\bigcup_{\alpha \in I} A_\alpha} = \{x : x \in A_\alpha \text{ for at least one set } A_\alpha \text{ with } \alpha \in I\}.\]

If $A_\alpha$ is a set for every $\alpha$ in some index set $I \neq \varnothing$, then
\[\emph{\bigcap_{\alpha \in I} A_\alpha} = \{x : x \in A_\alpha \text{ for every set } A_\alpha \text{ with } \alpha \in I\}.\]
A statement is a well-formed sentence or mathematical expression that is either true or false.
A propositional function is a well-formed expression, containing variables, which becomes a statement upon substitution of these variables with appropriate values.
A logical operator (or connective) on mathematical statements is a word or combination of words that combines one or more mathematical statements to make a new statement.
A compound statement is a statement that contains one or more operators.
Given statements $P$ and $Q$ then the converse of $P \Rightarrow Q$ is $Q \Rightarrow P$.
Given statements $P$ and $Q$ then the inverse of $P \Rightarrow Q$ is $\neg P \Rightarrow \neg Q$.
Two statements $P$ and $Q$ are considered logically equivalent, $P \equiv Q$, if the truth tables yield the same outcomes for corresponding input values of component statements.
Given statements $P$ and $Q$, then the contrapositive of the conditional statement $P \Rightarrow Q$ is $\neg Q \Rightarrow \neg P$.
The symbol $\forall$ is called the universal quantifier. $\forall$ stands for the phrase \textit{“For all”} or \textit{“For every"}, or \textit{“For each"}.
The symbol $\exists$ is called the existential quantifier. $\exists$ stands for the phrase \textit{“There exists a"} or \textit{“There is a"}.
An integer $n$ is even if $n = 2a$ for some integer $a$.
An integer $n$ is odd if $n = 2a+1$ for some integer $a$.
Parity is the attribute of an integer being either even or odd.
Suppose $a$ and $b$ are integers. We say that $a$ divides $b$, written $a \mid b$, if $b = ac$ for some $c \in \Z$.
A number $n \in \Z^+$ is prime if it has exactly two unique positive integer divisors, 1 and $n$.
A number $n \in \Z^+$ is composite if it has more than two positive integer divisors.
The greatest common divisor of integers $a$ and $b$, denoted $\gcd(a,b)$, is the largest integer that divides both $a$ and $b$.
The least common multiple of nonzero integers $a$ and $b$, denoted $\operatorname{lcm}(a,b)$, is the smallest integer in $\Z^+$ that is a multiple of both $a$ and $b$.
Given integers $a$ and $b$ and $n \in \Z^{+}$, we say that $a$ and $b$ are congruent modulo$n$} if $n \mid (a-b)$. We express this as $a \equiv b \mod{n}$.
A real number $x$ is rational if $x = a\slash b$ for some $a,b \in \Z$.
A real number $x$ is irrational if it is not rational; that is, if $x \neq a\slash b$ for every $a,b \in \Z$.
Let $A$ and $B$ be sets. Then $A = B$ if $A \subseteq B$ and $B \subseteq A$.
A set $T$ that is a subset of $\mathbb{Z}$ is an inductive set provided that for each integer $k$, if $k \in T$, then $k+1 \in T$.
A relation on a set $A$ is a subset $R \subseteq A \times A$. We often abbreviate the statement $(x,y) \in R$ as $x \sim y$.
A relation $R$ is reflexive if $x \sim x$ for every $x\in A$.
A relation $R$ is symmetric if $x \sim y$ implies that $y \sim x$ for all $x,y \in A$.
A relation $R$ is transitive if when $x \sim y$ and $y \sim z$ then $x \sim z$ for all $x,y,z \in A$.
A relation $R$ is antisymmetric if when $x \sim y$ and $y \sim x$ then $x = y$.
A relation $R$ on a set $A$ is an equivalence relation if it is reflexive, symmetric and transitive.

Suppose $R$ is an equivalence relation on a set $A$. Given any element $a \in A$, the equivalence class containing$a$} is the subset $\{x \in A : x \sim a\}$ of $A$ consisting of all elements of $A$ that relate to $a$. This set is denote as $[a]$.
A partition of a set $A$ is a set of nonempty subsets of $A$ such that the union of all the subsets equals $A$, and the intersection of any two different subsets is empty.
A relation from a set $A$ to $B$ is a subset $R \subseteq A \times B$. We often abbreviate the statement $(x,y) \in R$ as $x \sim y$.

Suppose $A$ and $B$ are sets. A function or mapping $f$ from $A$ to $B$, denoted $f : A \rightarrow B$, is a relation $f \subseteq A \times B$ from $A$ to $B$, satisfying the property that for each $a,b \in A$, if $a = b$ and $(a,c),(b,d) \in f$ then $c = d$. The statement $(a,b) \in f$ is abbreviated $f(a) = b$.
Given some function $f : A \to B$, then the set $A$ is called the domain.
Given some function $f : A \to B$, then the set $B$ is called the codomain.
Given some function $f : A \to B$ the set \[f(A) = \{ f(a) : a \in A\} \subseteq B\] is called the range of $f$ or image of $A$ under $f$. Similarly $f(a) \in B$ is the image of $a$ under $f$.

Two functions $f$ and $g$ are equal provided that
  • The domain of $f$ equals the domain of $g$.
  • The codomain of $f$ equals the codomain of $g$.
  • For each $x$ in the domain of $f$ (which equals the domain of $g$), $f(x) = g(x)$.
A function $f: A \to B$ is injective if for all $a,a' \in A$, $f(a) = f(a')$ implies $a = a'$.
A function $f: A \to B$ is surjective if for every $b \in B$ there is an $a \in A$ with $f(a) = b$.
A function $f: A \to B$ is bijective if $f$ is both injective and surjective.

Suppose $f: A \to B$ and $g:B \to C$ are functions with the property that the codomain of $f$ equals the domain of $g$. The composition of $f$ with $g$ is another function, denoted $g \circ f : A \to C$ and defined as follows: If $x \in A$, then $(g\circ f)(x) = g(f(x))$.
Given a relation $R$ from $A$ to $B$, the inverse relation of $R$ is the relation from $B$ to $A$ defined as $R^{-1} = \{(y,x) : (x,y) \in R\}$.
For a set $A$, the identity function on $A$ is the function $\id_A: A \to A$ defined as $\id_A(x) = x$ for every $x \in A$.
A map $g: B \to A$ is an inverse function of $f: A \to B$ if $g \circ f = \id_A$ and $f\circ g = \id_B$.
A function is said to be invertible if it has an inverse. We usually write $f^{-1}$ for the inverse of $f$.
Suppose $f: A \to B$ is a function. If $Y \subset B$, the preimage of$Y$} is the set $f^{-1} = \{x \in A : f(x) \in Y\} \subseteq A$.

Two sets $A$ and $B$ are equipollent, or have the same cardinality, written $\abs{A} = \abs{B}$, if there exists a bijective function $f: A \to B$. If no such bijective function $f$ exists, then the sets are not equipollent, or have unequal cardinalities, written $\abs{A} \neq \abs{B}$.
Suppose $A$ is a set. Then $A$ is countably infinite if $\abs{N} = \abs{A}$, that is, if there exists a bijection $\N \to A$.
Suppose $A$ is a set. The set $A$ is countable if it is finite or countably infinite.
Suppose $A$ is a set. The set $A$ is uncountable if it is infinite and not equipollent with $\N$.
The cardinality of the natural numbers is denoted as $\aleph_0$. That is $\abs{\N} = \aleph_0$.
A statement in logic or mathematics is an assertion that is either true or false.

\[\begin{array}{ccc}
         A & \emph{\implies} & B \\ \hline
         T &     \textbf{T}    & T \\
         T &     \textbf{F}    & F \\
         F &     \textbf{T}    & T \\
         F &     \textbf{T}    & F 
         \end{array}
         \qquad
         \begin{array}{ccc}
         A & \emph{\wedge} & B \\ \hline
         T &     \textbf{T}    & T \\
         T &     \textbf{F}    & F \\
         F &     \textbf{F}    & T \\
         F &     \textbf{F}    & F 
         \end{array}
         \qquad
